name: Find who republished your press release with Bright Data, GPT-5.6 and Gmail drafts

parameters.content:
## Find who ran your announcement, including the ones who never named you

Searching your brand finds who talked about you. Searching your own sentences, verbatim, finds who used your words - which is a different and much shorter list.

### How it works

Paste the release URL into the form. Bright Data fetches it, and **`Pick The Fingerprints`** chooses the sentences nobody else would have written: executive quotes, specific numbers, named products. Boilerplate is scored down hard, because `"we are excited to announce the general availability"` returns ten different companies and none of them are you.

Each phrase is searched in quotes through the **SERP API**. Every page that comes back is fetched through the **Web Unlocker** and measured in code: what share of your wording survived verbatim, whether the page links to you at all, and whether your brand reached the headline. A phrase whose hits mostly do not mention you is thrown out as boilerplate and reported.

GPT-5.6 is asked only what the arithmetic cannot answer - the angle they took and what they cut. Outlets that used your words **without linking** get a follow-up prepared as a **Gmail draft**.

### Setup

1. Bright Data: a SERP zone and a Web Unlocker zone, as one Header Auth credential. The free tier is 5,000 credits a month with no card.

2. An OpenAI credential, a Gmail credential and a Slack credential.

3. Nothing else to configure. The form takes the release URL, your brand and your domain.

4. Open the form URL on the Form Trigger node and paste a release you published a week or two ago.

## 1. One release, pasted in
A form rather than a schedule. This is a question somebody asks two days after publishing, not a thing that runs on Mondays.

## 2. Fingerprint it
Six sentences nobody else would have written. Proper nouns, digits and quoted speech score up; boilerplate scores hard down.

## 3. Search your own words, in quotes
Google honours the quotes exactly. A phrase whose hits mostly fail to mention the brand is discarded here as boilerplate, however well it scored.

## 4. Read the pages, count the overlap
Five-word shingles against the release, plus a plain regex for the link. Neither needs a model, so neither gets one.

## 5. Ask only what arithmetic cannot answer
What angle they took, what they left out, and - only when there is no link - what a follow-up would say.

## 6. A draft, never a send
Outlets that used your words without linking get a Gmail draft with no recipient. A person reads it, addresses it, and decides.

## Nothing is sent, and no address is ever looked up

The follow-ups are created as **Gmail drafts with no recipient**. That is deliberate on both counts. A person reads the draft, decides whether the pickup is worth a reply at all, and types the address themselves.

There is no email-finding step anywhere in this workflow and one should not be added. Harvesting writers' addresses off the pages they wrote is not something to automate, and in several jurisdictions unsolicited outreach to an address collected that way is a legal problem rather than a growth tactic.

**Absence of a link is not misconduct.** Plenty of outlets have a house policy against linking, ran it from a wire, or linked to a different page of yours than the one you searched. Read the article before you write to anyone about it.
